# Survival Basics — Burning Man 2026 (from the official Survival Guide, survival.burningman.org)

Black Rock City (BRC) is a temporary city built in Nevada's remote Black Rock Desert for Burning Man. Every participant is responsible for their own survival, safety, comfort, and well-being, and for Leaving No Trace. There is almost nothing for sale in the city (see Practical FAQs file): you must bring everything you need. [2026-confirmed]

## Water and hydration [2026-confirmed]
- Bring 1.5 gallons of water per person per day, covering drinking, washing, and cleaning.
- Water must be potable, from sources approved by the Nevada State Health Division.
- Always carry a full reusable water bottle when leaving camp.
- Dehydration symptoms: headaches, stomach cramps, constipation, flu-like symptoms, mood swings.
- Alcohol, caffeine, and drugs all increase dehydration risk. Electrolyte replacement helps alongside plain water.

## Heat and sun [2026-confirmed]
- Daytime temperatures routinely exceed 100°F (38°C). Overnight lows can reach the 40s°F (single digits °C).
- Elevation is nearly 4,000 feet, so skin burns faster and more severely than at sea level.
- Apply sunscreen every morning and reapply as needed; bring lip balm and lotion.
- Build shade structures for camp; rest during the hottest part of the day.
- Wide-brim hat recommended, with a chinstrap for wind.

## Dust and wind [2026-confirmed]
- Desert winds can exceed 75 mph and cause instant whiteouts (zero-visibility dust storms).
- Always carry a dust mask and goggles; goggles protect eyes during dust storms.
- If caught in a whiteout: seek shelter, sit down with your back to the wind, cover your face, and wait it out.

## Food [2026-confirmed]
- Bring all the food and beverages you will need for your whole stay.
- A cooking stove is optional, needed only if you plan to heat food or liquid.
- Ice is the only food-preservation item sold in the city (see Practical FAQs file).

## What to bring (Survival Guide packing list) [2026-confirmed]
- Good tent or shelter; warm sleeping bag and bedding; warm clothing; rain gear; sturdy footwear.
- 1.5 gal water/person/day; all food; reusable water bottle and cup.
- Dust mask and goggles; sunscreen; wide-brim hat.
- Extensive first-aid kit; hand sanitizer (60%+ alcohol); prescriptions in original containers; contact lens supplies.
- Flashlights/headlamps and spare batteries; bike lights and personal lights for night visibility (glow sticks are insufficient and become trash).
- Durable materials that will not break apart or scatter; aluminum cans for beverages (preferred over glass or plastic).
- A MOOP bag to carry everywhere; a pocket ashtray (e.g. mint tin) if you smoke.
- Tarps for kitchen/build/work areas; proper tie-downs for camp items and vehicle loads.
- Handled jug for daily MOOP collection around camp.
- Greywater containment system — no greywater may touch the playa.
- Secondary containment bins (e.g. kiddie pools) for any fuel containers.

## What to leave at home (MOOP-prone items) [2026-confirmed]
- Glitter, feathers, rhinestones, sequins, artificial grass.
- Wigs that shed, styrofoam coolers, plastic bags, loose paper, string, plastic cups.
- Hay, straw, gravel; plastic drink containers when avoidable.
- Everything you bring can become Matter Out of Place (MOOP) and must go home with you.

## Culture basics [evergreen]
- Burning Man is guided by the 10 Principles (see Ten Principles file).
- There is no money economy inside the city: no vending, no sponsorships, no advertising. Gifting is unconditional and expects nothing in return; Burning Man is not a barter economy.
- The Survival Guide's sections cover Culture, Transportation, City Infrastructure, Getting Around BRC, Survival/Health/Safety, Rules & Regulations, Kids & Families, Law Enforcement, and Leaving No Trace. A PDF version of the guide exists for offline reading.

# Event Logistics — Burning Man 2026

## Dates and theme [2026-confirmed]
- Burning Man 2026 runs Sunday, August 30 through Monday, September 7, 2026 (Labor Day), in the Black Rock Desert near Gerlach, Nevada.
- 2026 theme: "Axis Mundi" — celebrates interconnectedness, shared social realities, and ties to the natural world.
- The event officially ends Monday, September 7 at 6:00 pm; Exodus (departure) support continues through 11:59 pm Tuesday, September 8.
- Man burn: Saturday night, September 5; Temple burn: Sunday night, September 6. [2026 dates per multiple 2026 guides and the standard Saturday-Man/Sunday-Temple schedule; not stated on the BMorg pages fetched — treat exact burn times as unpublished]

## Gate [2026-confirmed unless noted]
- The Gate opens to all participants at 12:01 am on Sunday, August 30, 2026, and stays open 24 hours a day during the event.
- The Gate never "closes" for departures — there is no departure gate closure: the Gate is open around the clock, and you may leave whenever you like. You do NOT have to be off the playa before the event ends (Monday, September 7 at 6:00 pm) — Exodus support continues through 11:59 pm Tuesday, September 8. Only two things ever pause the Gate: bad weather (temporary) and a lost-child alert (outbound traffic held until the child is found, usually minutes).
- Every person needs a valid ticket; every vehicle except motorcycles needs a pre-purchased Vehicle Pass.
- Vehicle Passes cost $165 each plus taxes/fees, one per purchase in current sales. [2026-confirmed]
- 2026 Main Sale ticket tiers: $550, $675, $775, $975, $1,500, $3,000 ($775 approximates the per-participant cost). OMG (last-chance) Sale opened at noon July 29, 2026, registration from July 20. A final ticket sale was open as of August 2026 with no registration required.
- At the Gate, vehicles are searched and tickets are torn/scanned. Will Call/Box Office is reachable from any lane; "Apex" kiosks about 1/4 mile before the Gate direct Will Call traffic. Bring the whole vehicle to Will Call, not just one person.
- Box Office closes at 12:00 noon on September 7, 2026 — pick up tickets/credentials before then.
- Gate Road speed limit: 10 mph. Stay in your vehicle in line; no open containers of alcohol; do not walk in traffic lanes; keep headlights on at night if stopped on Highways 447 or 34.
- Wait times in the first 36 hours after opening can be 5+ hours. Shortest lines are typically 3–10 am on non-opening days; arriving Tuesday or later avoids the rush. The Gate can close temporarily in bad weather.
- Traffic info: BMIR 94.5 FM hourly traffic reports from opening Sunday; Gate Advisory Radio Station (GARS) 95.1 FM for entry-process updates; @BManTraffic on X/Twitter; BRC Dashboard at brcdashboard.burningman.org.

## Greeters [evergreen]
- The Greeters are the volunteer crew stationed just past the Gate on the way into the city — Black Rock City's official welcome. Every arriving vehicle rolls through the Greeters station after tickets are checked.
- What they do: welcome arrivals home ("Welcome home!" is the traditional greeting), orient newcomers to the city, hand out the WhatWhereWhen event booklet and city map, and answer arrival questions — where your camp's address is, how to find Playa Info or Center Camp.
- First-timers (playa "virgins") are traditionally invited to ring the big bell and make a dust angel on the playa.
- The Greeters station is also the city's arrival-side landmark: hitchhikers wait there, and Exodus directions reference it.
- Greeters are not the Gate: the Gate crew checks tickets and searches vehicles; the Greeters welcome and orient — no ticket business at Greeters.

## Early arrival [2026-confirmed]
- Arriving before Gate opening requires a pre-approved early arrival pass (Setup Access Pass) for each person; without one, the entire vehicle is turned away and sent back toward Reno.
- Do not wait in Gerlach or along Highways 447/34 before the Gate opens. Early-window arrivals are directed down Gate Road to an opening-night staging lot.
- Burner Express bus passengers arriving before Sunday's opening do not need a Setup Access Pass; Burner Express Air passengers arriving the Saturday before opening also do not need one.

## Burner Express [2026-confirmed]
- Burner Express Bus runs from San Francisco and Reno to Black Rock City; faster entry and exit than private vehicles; optional reserved camping near the on-playa bus depot; riders may pre-buy up to 20 gallons of water per person, collected at the Bus Depot on arrival. Tickets go on sale mid-May, are non-transferable and non-refundable, and require a BRC ticket to ride. Schedule: burnerexpress.burningman.org.
- Burner Express Air flies from Reno, the Bay Area, and Southern California into BRC's airport; same 20-gallon water option (collected at the airport); tickets on sale early May and typically sell out fast; operates from a separate area of Reno-Tahoe International.
- Carpool matching: official board at spark.burningman.org; Reno Airport Rideshare via Air Playa Info near baggage claim.

## Exodus and the Pulse [2026-confirmed]
- Route out: take K Street toward 6:00, then follow signs onto Gate Road; all lanes are outbound during Exodus.
- Pulse procedure: vehicles stop and shut engines off; every hour, all vehicles advance one mile simultaneously. Pulsing does not change total departure time; it provides rest breaks and reduces idling.
- Peak waits: 6–9 hours from Greeters to the County Road 34 pavement, plus 2–3+ hours to Reno; allow up to 12 hours to reach Reno airport at peak. Most departures happen Sunday and Monday.
- Best departure windows: very early morning, late evening, or Tuesday before noon; avoid roughly 10 am–4 pm.
- Do not create alternate exits — leaving the route violates BLM rules, earns tickets, and sends you back to the end of the queue.
- F Lot ("Final Frontier") near the pavement is a reunification station and the last chance to secure your load; last porta-potties are at the F Lots.
- Lockout help is available via Playa Info; a tow service operates Saturday through Tuesday post-event (request at Playa Info). AAA and similar clubs will not enter the event site.
- Exodus radio: GARS 95.1 FM travel times several times hourly; BMIR 94.5 FM Exodus info.
- Tips: check load security (and your neighbors'), blow dust out of your engine air filter to prevent overheating, keep a spare key accessible, use the far lanes if your vehicle is struggling so tow crews can reach you. Hitchhikers should wait at Greeters.

# Black Rock City Geography and Addressing

## The clock-face grid [2026-confirmed for locations; layout evergreen]
- Black Rock City is laid out as a giant clock face: a semicircle of streets wrapped around the Man, which stands at the center.
- Radial streets are named for clock times (2:00 through 10:00, e.g. 3:00, 4:30, 7:30). The 6:00 axis runs from Center Camp straight to the Man; 12:00 points toward the Temple and deep playa. [clock range/axis orientation: evergreen]
- Annular (ring) streets are lettered outward from the center: the Esplanade is the innermost ring facing the open playa, then A, B, C ... through K.
- An address like "7:30 & G" means the intersection of the 7:30 radial street and the G ring street. To find it: follow any ring street to the 7:30 radial, or ride a radial out/in to the G ring. Lower letters are closer to the Esplanade/open playa; times near 6:00 are closer to Center Camp.
- Ring-street names change yearly with the art theme, but the letters A–K stay the addressing system. [evergreen]

## Key locations (2026 city plan) [2026-confirmed]
- The Man: center of the clock face, out on the open playa.
- The Temple: on the open playa beyond the Man along the 12:00 axis. [axis placement evergreen; porta-potty banks flank the Man along 3:00 and 9:00 per the 2026 plan]
- Center Camp Plaza: 6:15 & B (heart of the city's 6:00 neighborhood).
- Plazas: at 3:00, 4:30, 6:00, 7:30, and 9:00 on both B and G streets.
- Playa Info / Lost & Found: Esplanade & 5:45. Placement Headquarters: Esplanade & 5:45 area.
- Ranger HQ: Esplanade & 6:30; Ranger outposts at the 3:00 and 9:00 plazas.
- Medical: 3:00 & C, 9:00 & C, and the main Emergency Services (ESD) / Rampart station at 5:15 & Esplanade. Ranger HQ is the one at 6:30 & Esplanade — different address.
- Arctica ice: Center Camp Plaza, 3:00 & G, 9:00 & G, bulk at 6:15 & K.
- Yellow Bike Shop (community bikes): 5:30 & D. Recycle Camp (aluminum cans): 5:35 & Esplanade.
- Burn Gardens: Esplanade & 5:30, in front of MOOP Map HQ.
- Airport (88NV): follow the 5:00 direction out toward the perimeter fence. Box Offices at the Main Gate and the Airport.

## Camping zones [2026-confirmed]
- Main camping: the semicircle between Esplanade and K.
- Open camping (first-come): between H and K streets.
- Walk-in camping: past K Street between 2:00 and 5:00 — no vehicles.
- Placed theme camps occupy most frontage on the Esplanade, plazas, and inner streets. [evergreen]

## Open playa and deep playa [evergreen; buffer 2026-confirmed]
- The open playa (inside the Esplanade arc) is reserved for interactive art — no camping.
- "Deep playa" is the far open area beyond the Temple toward the trash fence, sparser and darker; large art and few landmarks.
- The whole city sits inside a pentagon-shaped perimeter "trash fence"; crossing it is prohibited. The Bureau of Land Management maintains a no-camping buffer zone outside the fence.
- Porta-potty banks throughout the city and on the open playa are marked at night by solar-powered blue lights.

## Navigation tips [evergreen]
- At night, orient by the Man and the lit Esplanade arc; the Temple marks 12:00.
- Ask anyone — giving directions by clock-and-letter is universal ("we're at 7:30 & G, toward the 7:30 plaza").
- The city holds roughly 80,000 people at peak.

# The 10 Principles of Burning Man [evergreen — verbatim from burningman.org]

Burning Man co-founder Larry Harvey wrote the 10 Principles in 2004 as guidelines for the newly-formed Regional Network. They were crafted not as a dictate of how people should be and act, but as a reflection of the community's ethos and culture as it had organically developed since the event's inception.

## Principle 1: Radical Inclusion

"Anyone may be a part of Burning Man. We welcome and respect the stranger. No prerequisites exist for participation in our community."

## Principle 2: Gifting

"Burning Man is devoted to acts of gift giving. The value of a gift is unconditional. Gifting does not contemplate a return or an exchange for something of equal value."

## Principle 3: Decommodification

"In order to preserve the spirit of gifting, our community seeks to create social environments that are unmediated by commercial sponsorships, transactions, or advertising. We stand ready to protect our culture from such exploitation. We resist the substitution of consumption for participatory experience."

## Principle 4: Radical Self-reliance

"Burning Man encourages the individual to discover, exercise and rely on their inner resources."

## Principle 5: Radical Self-expression

"Radical self-expression arises from the unique gifts of the individual. No one other than the individual or a collaborating group can determine its content. It is offered as a gift to others. In this spirit, the giver should respect the rights and liberties of the recipient."

## Principle 6: Communal Effort

"Our community values creative cooperation and collaboration. We strive to produce, promote and protect social networks, public spaces, works of art, and methods of communication that support such interaction."

## Principle 7: Civic Responsibility

"We value civil society. Community members who organize events should assume responsibility for public welfare and endeavor to communicate civic responsibilities to participants. They must also assume responsibility for conducting events in accordance with local, state and federal laws."

## Principle 8: Leaving No Trace

"Our community respects the environment. We are committed to leaving no physical trace of our activities wherever we gather. We clean up after ourselves and endeavor, whenever possible, to leave such places in a better state than when we found them."

## Principle 9: Participation

"Our community is committed to a radically participatory ethic. We believe that transformative change, whether in the individual or in society, can occur only through the medium of deeply personal participation. We achieve being through doing. Everyone is invited to work. Everyone is invited to play. We make the world real through actions that open the heart."

## Principle 10: Immediacy

"Immediate experience is, in many ways, the most important touchstone of value in our culture. We seek to overcome barriers that stand between us and a recognition of our inner selves, the reality of those around us, participation in society, and contact with a natural world exceeding human powers. No idea can substitute for this experience."

Note: the ordering above (Radical Inclusion, Gifting, Decommodification, Radical Self-reliance, Radical Self-expression, Communal Effort, Civic Responsibility, Leaving No Trace, Participation, Immediacy) is the official burningman.org order, cross-checked against Burners Without Borders and the Burning Man Journal. The principle text has been stable since Larry Harvey wrote it in 2004.

# Safety, Medical, and Rangers — Black Rock City 2026

## Medical stations [2026-confirmed]
- Locations: 3:00 & C, 9:00 & C, and the main station at 5:15 & Esplanade. Look for the lighted red cross above each station.
- The 5:15 & Esplanade site is the city's main medical center: the Emergency Services Department (ESD) station and the Rampart Emergency Care Center are co-located there. Plaza stations handle walk-in first aid; serious cases go to the main station, and critical patients are flown/driven to Reno hospitals (off-playa transport is at the patient's expense). [2026-confirmed: Survival Guide "On-Playa Resources", "Health", and "Consent" pages all say 5:15 & Esplanade; the "Getting Help" page's "Esplanade near 6:30" is Ranger HQ's address, not medical. Transport/cost detail: evergreen, UNVERIFIED for 2026]
- Playa foot: cracked, burning skin on your feet from the alkaline dust — very common. Soak 20 minutes a day in a 4:1 water-to-vinegar mix, then lotion and socks; closed shoes and socks prevent it. Treat yourself or your campmates first (camp first-aid kit); if it is worse than you can manage, go to a medical station. [2026-confirmed: Survival Guide "Health"]
- Medical help can also be summoned through any Ranger, staff member with a radio, or BRC 911 (see Radio file).

## Black Rock Rangers [2026-confirmed]
- Veteran Burners who volunteer to help participants resolve conflicts and find solutions. They are not police.
- Recognize them by khaki attire with the Burning Man logo and white hats with the Ranger logo.
- They mediate disagreements, locate lost children, address safety concerns, direct people to resources, and can radio for law enforcement, medical, mental health, fire, or environmental teams.
- Available 24/7. Ranger HQ: Esplanade & 6:30. Ranger outposts: 3:00 and 9:00 plazas. Pairs patrol the whole city on foot/bike.
- High Rock Security: contract security team in black "High Rock Security" shirts supporting the Rangers; they prefer de-escalation and escalate serious issues to law enforcement.

## Emergencies [2026-confirmed]
- Flag down a Ranger, law enforcement, or any event staff/volunteer with a radio; or go to a Ranger outpost or medical station.
- BRC 911 Dispatch by personal radio: 451.9000 MHz, CTCSS/PL tone 91.5.
- Urgent messages from the outside world: email 911@burningman.org (delivered by Rangers); check Playa Info in Center Camp for incoming messages.
- Before arriving, make sure your people at home know: your full legal name and playa name, camp name/location, vehicle description and plate, and unique identifying features — that is what searchers use.

## Lost & Found [2026-confirmed]
- Location: Playa Info at Esplanade & 5:45. Database searchable 24/7; item pickup 9 am–6 pm.
- Label everything with your name to improve recovery odds. Lost & Found does not accept bicycles.
- After the event, lost & found moves online/to Reno via Playa Info's published process. [evergreen, UNVERIFIED 2026 details]

## Lost child protocol [evergreen — sourced from BMorg journal and Ranger practice]
- If your child is missing: go to the nearest Ranger immediately (Ranger HQ at 6:30 & Esplanade, outposts at 3:00 and 9:00 plazas, or any patrolling pair).
- Rangers initiate a Lost Child protocol: an all-hands alert to law enforcement and infrastructure staff, citizen alerts on BMIR, and the Gate closes to outbound traffic (including airport departures) until the child is found — usually within minutes.
- Teach children: if separated, find a Ranger (khaki, white hat) or any staff member with a radio, and stay put in a lit, public place.
- F.U.N. (Family Unification Network) program: register children at Ranger HQ (Esplanade & 6:30); each child gets a wristband with a unique serial number linked to guardians and camp location, so any Ranger can arrange a fast reunion.
- Kids 12 and under attend free but require a Kid's Ticket. [2026-confirmed]

## Whiteouts / dust storms [2026-confirmed protocol]
- Winds over 75 mph can drop visibility to zero within seconds.
- On foot or bike: stop, seek shelter if immediately available, otherwise sit down with your back to the wind and cover your face; put on your goggles and dust mask (carry them always); wait it out — whiteouts usually pass in minutes.
- Driving in a whiteout: stop the vehicle and wait; do not creep forward blind. [evergreen]

## Trip hazards, rebar, night visibility
- Rebar and tent stakes: hammer rebar fully into the ground where possible; cover any exposed stake ends with tennis balls, plastic bottles, or padding; candy-cane (bent-top) rebar reduces snag risk. Tripping on rebar and guy-lines is a classic playa injury. Mark guy-lines and stakes with lights or bright tape at night. [evergreen — sourced from burningman.org Rebar Safety page and community guides]
- Night visibility: the city is unlit and full of bikes and art cars. Wear lights after dark — EL wire, LED strings, headlamps, bike head- and tail-lights. A person or bike moving in the dark with no lights is called a "darkwad" and is a genuine collision hazard. Glow sticks are considered insufficient and become trash. [evergreen; bike-light rules 2026-confirmed]
- Handheld lasers are banned in BRC; mounted lasers require licensing/compliance. Drones are forbidden without prior registration and pre-flight tagging by the Safety Team. [2026-confirmed]
- Secure valuables, especially on Burn night (locking them in your car is suggested); photograph serial numbers in case a police report is needed. [2026-confirmed]
- Climbing on art: only where the artist explicitly allows it; structures are engineered for wind/load, not always for climbers. [evergreen]

# Radio in Black Rock City

## Official stations [2026-confirmed]
- BMIR 94.5 FM — Burning Man Information Radio. Broadcasts travel, emergency, and general information plus community programming 24 hours a day. Hourly Gate traffic reports start opening Sunday; Exodus-specific info at event end.
- GARS 95.1 FM — Gate Advisory Radio Station. Gate Road travel times and traffic reports several times an hour, plus entry-process updates.
- BRC 911 Dispatch (emergencies only, two-way): 451.9000 MHz with CTCSS/PL tone 91.5 programmed into a personal radio reaches Black Rock City's 911 dispatch.

## Camp-band radio culture [evergreen — community practice from ePlaya and radio forums]
- Many camps carry FRS/GMRS handhelds ("family radios") for coordination. FRS range on playa is limited (roughly half a mile); GMRS at higher power reaches from camp to deep playa; MURS (2 W) is quiet on playa and can reach much farther with a vehicle antenna.
- Etiquette: listen before transmitting; open with the name of the person/camp you're calling so others know the traffic isn't for them; keep transmissions short — channels are shared citywide.
- CTCSS "privacy" codes filter incoming chatter so a camp mostly hears its own crew (they do not make the channel private — others can still hear you).
- GMRS legally requires an FCC license; adding external antennas to FRS radios is illegal.
- The Emergency Services Department does not coordinate FRS/GMRS bands, but high-power radio setups should be reported to ESD in advance so signals can be isolated if interference occurs.
- Practical tips: agree on a camp channel+code before arrival, write it on the camp board, keep radios in ziplocks against dust, bring 12 V/solar charging. [evergreen]

# MOOP, Greywater, Burn Scars, and Fire Safety

## MOOP basics [2026-confirmed]
- MOOP = Matter Out of Place: any material left on the desert surface that didn't come from the playa — from couches down to glitter, sequins, wood chips, and hair.
- Black Rock City is the largest Leave No Trace event in the world; there are no trash cans — everyone packs out everything they bring in.
- Carry a MOOP bag everywhere; do a daily MOOP sweep of your camp with a handled jug; secure loose items and costume pieces before they blow away.
- Line sweeps: camps walk shoulder-to-shoulder across their footprint picking every fragment — do one before leaving. [evergreen practice]
- The MOOP Map: after the event, the Playa Restoration team surveys every square meter of the city footprint and publishes a color-coded map (green = clean, yellow/red = problem areas) scoring each camp's location. Red scores can cost a camp its placement the following year. MOOP Map HQ is at Esplanade & 5:30. [map mechanics evergreen; HQ location 2026-confirmed]
- The event's federal permit depends on passing BLM's post-event site inspection. [evergreen]

## Greywater and blackwater [2026-confirmed]
- No greywater (wash water) may ever touch the playa — not even "just soapy water." Even treated greywater must be properly disposed of.
- Disposal options: small-footprint evaporation ponds, hauling to off-site RV dump stations, or contracting United Site Services (USS) for on-site pumping (pumping may arrive a day later than scheduled — plan capacity accordingly).
- Spill response: (1) stop the source — no more showers/dishes/toilets until fixed; (2) collect leaked fluid with buckets and dig up contaminated playa if it fits in a 5-gallon bucket; (3) repair or get pumped (flag USS trucks marked "RV"); (4) report any spill over 25 gallons to Rangers or the Environmental Compliance/ESD team immediately — blackwater or fuel spills over 25 gallons are environmental emergencies.
- Vehicle leaks: check your undercarriage daily (old RVs especially); use drip pans, tarps, or secured plywood under drips; excavate and pack out contaminated playa, then refill the hole. Leaky vehicles should be fixed before arriving.

## Fuel safety [2026-confirmed]
- Camp fuel storage cap: no more than 110 gallons or two 55-gallon drums per camp.
- Fill containers to at most 80% (heat expansion). Never set fuel containers directly on the playa, even briefly.
- All fuel containers need secondary containment holding 110% of the largest container's volume, in place before fuel is unpacked.
- Questions: fuelsafety@burningman.org.

## Burn scars and burning responsibly [2026-confirmed]
- Never burn directly on the playa: it bakes the surface into a dark, brick-like scar that lasts years and creates hazardous bumps. Volunteers have spent thousands of hours cleaning historical burn scars.
- Burn barrels: elevated at least 6 inches off the playa, contained; unpainted wood only; small amounts of paper/cardboard as kindling only with a wire-mesh ember cover. Violations risk BLM confiscation for the rest of the event.
- Never burn trash, treated/painted wood, or anything that isn't yours to burn.
- Bring a shovel and metal containers to remove your ashes; ash disposal is your responsibility.
- Community Burn Gardens (public burn platforms): Esplanade & 5:30, open Sunday Sept 6 (10 am) through Tuesday Sept 8; wood donations accepted; no cardboard, paper, compost, recycling, trash, or toxic materials.
- Art burns and the big burns happen on protected burn platforms with Fire Art Safety Team (FAST) oversight and fire perimeters — respect the perimeter until it drops. [evergreen]

## Packing out and heading home [2026-confirmed]
- Precycle before arriving: strip packaging at home, favor aluminum cans, avoid glass and styrofoam.
- Recycle Camp at 5:35 & Esplanade takes aluminum cans only (9 am–5 pm); everything else leaves with you.
- Secure your load for Exodus — highway-side MOOP from unsecured loads is a major issue; use the F Lot stop to re-check straps.
- Use legitimate trash/recycling/RV-dump locations in Nevada (the guide lists them); do not dump in Gerlach, Empire, or roadside bins.

# Practical FAQs — Burning Man 2026

## Ice (Arctica) [2026-confirmed]
- Locations: Center Camp Plaza ("Ice Main"), 3:00 & G ("Ice Cubed"), 9:00 & G ("Ice Nine"), and bulk sales at the Large Order Outpost, 6:15 & K (the only location with non-ADA vehicle parking).
- 2026 hours: pre-event Aug 27–30: 12–5 pm; event week Aug 31–Sep 6: 10 am–5 pm (Sep 6: 12–5 pm); Exodus Monday Sep 7: 10 am–12 pm.
- Payment: the Center Camp, 3:00, and 9:00 igloos take credit cards, tap/Apple Pay, and cash; the Large Order Outpost is cash-free.
- Price: not published on the pages fetched; recent years ran about $10 per bag. [UNVERIFIED for 2026]
- Ice sales are the city's only retail commerce (plus airport fees); proceeds have traditionally benefited local communities. [latter point evergreen, UNVERIFIED 2026]

## Center Camp coffee [status confirmed through 2026 guide]
- The Center Camp Café stopped selling coffee and drinks after the 2022 decommodification/sustainability decision; nothing has replaced the sales. The 2026 Survival Guide lists no beverage commerce — ice is the only thing sold in the city.
- Center Camp remains a large shaded gathering space with performances, art, and community programming ("re-centered" as a non-commercial heart of the city since 2023–24). Bring your own coffee setup or find a camp gifting it.

## Bikes [2026-confirmed]
- The four rules: Light it, Lock it, Label it (camp name + address), and Limit speed to 5 mph (including e-bikes).
- Best playa bikes: fat-tire cruisers or mountain bikes; skinny road tires fail in soft playa. Simple single-speeds survive dust better than derailleurs and cable brakes. Arrive with the bike in working order — repair camps have limited capacity.
- Lights: headlight (aimed so it doesn't blind), red tail light, plus decorative lighting so you can find it parked. Unlit riders are "darkwads."
- Never lock a bike to guy wires or structures. Secure decorations so they don't shed MOOP.
- Community bikes (bright green): free, short one-way trips only; never lock, keep at camp, decorate, or take home; report broken ones to the Yellow Bike Shop at 5:30 & D.
- Over 1,700 bikes were abandoned in 2024 — take yours home or donate it properly; abandonment violates Leave No Trace.

## Porta-potty etiquette [evergreen]
- Only human waste and single-ply toilet paper go in the potty. If it didn't come out of your body (plus single-ply TP), it doesn't go in — wipes, tampons, trash, and multi-ply paper jam the pump trucks and get banks taken out of service.
- Sit rather than hover; hovering makes messes. Close the lid, keep the door latched against wind.
- Potty banks are marked at night by solar blue lights; last outbound potties during Exodus are at the F Lots.
- Peeing on the playa is prohibited (it's public land and it's MOOP).

## Sun, moon, and temperatures for event week (Aug 30 – Sep 7, 2026)

## Cameras, photography, photos, and consent [2026-confirmed]
- Photography rules: as a condition of entry, participants agree to ASK PERMISSION before photographing or recording anyone. Ask first — every time, everyone.
- Images from Black Rock City may not be used for any commercial, promotional, editorial, or otherwise non-personal purpose unless the photographer registered as professional media in advance and received permission from Burning Man Project.
- Permitted professional media are credentialed and their cameras carry a unique Media ID tag. If someone is being disrespectful with a camera, note their Media # and bring it to Media Mecca (6:15 & Esplanade); if they have no Media Tag, find a Black Rock Ranger immediately.
- Drones/UAVs must be pre-registered; if you are not sure you have permission to bring a drone, you don't — leave it at home.
- If your picture or your images turn up used without permission: press@burningman.org.

## Dogs and other animals [2026-confirmed]
- Dogs and other animals — including emotional-support animals — are NOT permitted at the event. Show up with an animal and you will not be admitted. The only exception is a service animal trained to perform a task for a person's disability.
- Black Rock City is loud, hot, and frightening for animals; the rule protects them as much as people.

## Hot springs and packages [2026-confirmed]
- Local hot springs are OFF LIMITS during the event under the BLM permit (some are lethally hot); the BLM patrols them.
- Do not ship packages to Burning Man's Gerlach office or PO Box — they are returned. USPS General Delivery, Gerlach, NV 89412 works for a package to yourself; nothing can be delivered to you on playa.

# Veteran Techniques — curated from Burn.Life [evergreen unless tagged]

This section summarizes field-tested build and living techniques from Burn.Life, a
non-commercial hobbyist Burning Man site written by veteran burner Dr. Yes. The
knowledge below is restated in Playa Pal's own words with per-topic credit; the full
guides live at burn.life and are worth reading before the burn. Where a Burn.Life
number differs from the official 2026 Survival Guide, the official number wins (see
the Water and Hydration section: the ration is 1.5 gallons per person per day).
Prices and vendor details from the source era are tagged [era: 2014-2016 — verify].

*Credit: [Burn.Life](https://www.burn.life/) (Dr. Yes). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## Anchoring: lag screws instead of rebar [evergreen technique]
- Veteran alternative to rebar for staking tents, shade structures, and tarps: hex-head
  lag screws driven straight into the playa with a cordless drill (impact driver best,
  regular drill fine) and a 3/8" socket bit. No pilot hole — tight packing grips.
- Sizing: 3/8" hex-head lag screws, sold in 10", 12", 14". 12" held a large shade
  structure through storms. Monkey-hut ribs are the exception — they still want ~24"
  rebar (the PVC rib slides over 8-10" of exposed rebar).
- Anchor point trick: before driving, thread the screw through one link of a 2-link
  chain segment. Use chain thick enough that the screw passes but the hex head does
  not — the head pins link 1 flush to the ground and link 2 becomes your anchor loop
  (no washers needed). Buy 3 chain links per screw; cut every third link off-playa.
- Why over rebar: sits flush (no shin-spearing trip hazard), needs no guy-lines of its
  own, goes in and out in ~5 seconds, reusable for years, similar cost.
- Leaving: unscrew, bag, done. Charge drill batteries fully; bring spares.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — Lag Screws 101](https://www.burn.life/lag-screws-101.html) (Dr. Yes, curating a guide by u/ApesInSpace; technique by FIGJAM). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## Anchoring: rebar, if you must [evergreen technique]
- Where rebar still makes sense (monkey-hut ribs, or you already own it): use 18" or
  24" lengths in the #4 size (about 1/2" thick), driven fully in.
- Drive it with a metal-head mallet — plastic mallets get chewed apart by rebar.
- Cover every exposed end: cut a slit in a tennis ball and push it on. Exposed rebar
  ends have opened real ankles; a fall onto bare rebar can injure badly.
- Removal trick: clamp locking vice-grip pliers a few inches above the base, then
  lever against a piece of 2x4 to walk the bar out of the ground.
- The stakes bundled with a cheap tent will bend and pull out in a real playa blow.
  If weak stakes are all you have, keep something dense inside the tent (a loaded
  cooler works) so a collapsed tent at least stays on the ground instead of flying.
- A tent loose in a windstorm is a hazard to the whole neighborhood, not just to you.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — Tents and Shade](https://www.burn.life/tents-and-shade.html) and [Lag Screws 101](https://www.burn.life/lag-screws-101.html) (Dr. Yes; lag-screw technique by FIGJAM). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## Shade: Aluminet, shade cloth, carports [evergreen technique]
- Effectiveness ladder: full carport/canopy frame > woven shade cloth > Aluminet;
  portability and setup ease run the other way.
- Aluminet (woven reflective mesh) over the tent is the easy big win: it reflects
  solar load instead of absorbing it. It comes in strengths — 70% is the strongest
  commonly sold and worth it. Result reported: sleeping until 10:30-11am inside a tent
  that would otherwise be an oven by 8:30.
- A carport-style canopy (the common 10'x20' class) over the whole tent is the gold
  standard — light steel frame, heavy fabric ceiling, optional walls — but bulky, and
  it MUST be staked like you mean it (see Anchoring). Playa windstorms destroy
  casually-staked canopies.
- A monkey hut (PVC-rib quonset over rebar) is as good as a carport and cheaper if
  you are willing to build it.
- Whatever the shade, the tent under it still needs a strong metal frame and serious
  stakes or lag screws — bundled big-box stakes fail exactly when the storm hits.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — Tents and Shade](https://www.burn.life/tents-and-shade.html) (Dr. Yes). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## Shade: canopy wind safety and cooling the tent [evergreen technique]
- Canopy walls act as sails: side panels that do not pass wind can turn the whole
  structure into a kite. Guy-wire canopies aggressively; the winds reach gale force.
- The cheap 10'x10' pop-up shades are cheap for a reason. If one comes anyway, anchor
  it with multiple guy lines and deeply driven stakes or lag screws, never its own
  feet alone.
- Cooling options inside a tent, in rising order of effort: battery or plug-in fans;
  a swamp cooler; an air conditioner if your camp grid or generator can power it
  (vent it properly).
- Swamp coolers love the playa: they need exactly what the desert has — bone-dry air —
  plus air circulation. The classic DIY design is FIGJAM's bucket cooler. Reported
  field result: it could not chill a whole Shiftpod's airspace, but ducting its cool
  air under the bed sheets was almost too cold. Aim the cold at the sleeper, not the
  room.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — Tents and Shade](https://www.burn.life/tents-and-shade.html) (Dr. Yes; bucket-cooler design by FIGJAM). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## Shelter: choosing a playa tent [evergreen technique]
- What matters, in order: sturdiness (strong metal frame + serious anchoring — winds
  reach gale force), dust-sealing, waterproofing (real rainstorms do happen), interior
  height you can stand in, and zippers strong enough to yank when dust cakes them.
- Dust-sealing test: every mesh opening needs a solid fabric flap that zips over it.
  Mesh-only panels mean everything inside wears a visible dust layer after one storm.
  Mesh can be retrofitted: sew or tape solid fabric over it.
- Canvas tents win on the playa if the budget allows: heavier, far more dust- and
  wind-resistant, genuinely rain-proof, and they last decades with care.
- Two proven picks from years of use: the Kodiak 10'x14' canvas cabin tent (stand-up
  height, excellent build, overhead storage, near dust-proof sealed up) and the
  Shiftpod 2 (roughly twice the Kodiak's price; sets up and tears down in minutes,
  roomier vertical walls, built-in ports for AC or swamp-cooler ducting).
- The Shiftpod's reflective skin still wants real shade over it; treat "reflective"
  as a bonus, not a shade plan.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — Tents and Shade](https://www.burn.life/tents-and-shade.html) (Dr. Yes). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## Shelter: sleeping clean and organized [evergreen technique]
- Elevate the bed: a camping bed frame keeps the mattress off the floor, which keeps
  the daily dust film off your bedding, opens bin storage underneath, and simply
  feels more like a real bed at 4am.
- Cover the sleeping surface with a plain sheet during the day; whatever dust sneaks
  in lands on the sheet, not the pillow. Shake it out at night.
- Shoes stay outside the door — wearing them in is the fastest way to coat the tent.
- Live out of tubs or plastic drawer sets; a tent you can find things in feels twice
  as big by Thursday.
- Keep the constantly-grabbed items (sunscreen, sunglasses, goggles) in a pocket
  right at the tent entrance so nobody tracks dust in to fetch them.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — Tents and Shade](https://www.burn.life/tents-and-shade.html) (Dr. Yes). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## Coolers: making ice last the week [evergreen technique]
- Freeze large 2.5-liter square-ish drinking-water bottles at home and load them in as
  your ice. Reported result: still ice a week later — and the melt is drinking water,
  not a soggy food bath.
- Pre-cool every beverage before it goes in; warm cans burn ice fast.
- Open the cooler as rarely as possible. Keep it in shade, always.
- Elevate it off the playa on a couple of pieces of wood — ground contact is a big
  heat leak.
- Cheap cooler upgrade: tape reflective insulation tightly around the whole body
  (double layer, smallest possible gap at the lid), or just wrap it in a quilt.
- Premium coolers (Yeti/Engel/Pelican class) genuinely perform: a 65-qt example ran
  Saturday load-out to Thursday on playa before needing Arctica ice.
- Pace the menu around the cooler: eat fresh food early in the week, frozen food late.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — Food and Water](https://www.burn.life/food-and-water.html) (Dr. Yes). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## Menu: eating when it is too hot to be hungry [evergreen technique]
- Appetite shrinks on playa. A realistic pattern: one real meal a day plus nutritious
  snacks, and lots of water. Eat anyway — the body still needs fuel.
- Salt matters: you sweat it out all day, so salty food is both needed and tastes
  right out there.
- Boil-in-bag is the tent-camp power move: cook stews, curries, or meatballs at home,
  seal them in bags, then boil the bag on a small propane stove and eat from it — no
  dishes. Freeze-dried camping meals (Mountain House class) work the same way.
- Instant oatmeal owns breakfast: boiling water is the whole recipe.
- A big pasta salad with meat or tofu keeps all week in the cooler and covers lunch.
- Soup works — and if the stove feels like too much, cold soup is honestly fine there.
- Squeeze pouches of apple sauce or quality baby food, kept cold, go down easily when
  nothing else sounds appealing. Nuts, hard cheese, and nut butter carry the between
  hours. Fresh fruit and vegetables feel like luxury by mid-week — bring some.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — Food and Water](https://www.burn.life/food-and-water.html) and [Burning on a Budget](https://www.burn.life/burning-on-a-budget.html) (Dr. Yes). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## Bikes: playa-proofing and not losing it [evergreen technique]
- The right playa bike is cheap, comfortable (beach-cruiser posture), and wears fat
  tires for soft playa. Single-speed is fine — the city is flat, and gears are just
  more parts for dust to kill. Playa dust is corrosive; most burners keep a dedicated
  playa bike and simply store it dirty between years.
- Tennis-ball trick: slice a hole in a tennis ball and push it onto the kickstand
  foot. Otherwise soft playa swallows the kickstand and the bike falls over.
- Write your name, camp, and playa address on a slip of paper and seal it to the
  frame with clear packing tape — the honest way lost or "enthusiastically borrowed"
  bikes come home the next morning.
- Decorate distinctively (fur, fabric, zip ties) — it is self-expression AND the only
  way to find yours in a rack of hundreds. Lights at night: to be seen, and to find it.
- Add a front or rear basket if you will be hauling ice from Arctica.
- Lock it, but NEVER to art unless the piece is explicitly marked for bike parking.
  At big burns and sound camps, lock up a short walk away — the crowd grows and
  swallows whatever is parked at the center. Steer around soft dust piles.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — Bikes](https://www.burn.life/bikes.html) (Dr. Yes). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## Clothing: playa foot and the always-carry three [evergreen technique]
- Feet first: constant exposure to the alkaline dust cracks skin until it can bleed —
  the dreaded playa foot. Closed shoes or boots with socks, day and night, prevent
  it. Choose comfort over costume for footwear; you will walk miles.
- Pack two pairs of socks and underwear for every day. Fresh socks when everything
  else is dusty is one of the event's small miracles.
- Never leave camp without the three: goggles that seal around the eyes (whiteouts
  arrive fast), a dust mask (a bandana over the mouth genuinely works), and water —
  a hands-free carrier like a hydration pack beats any bottle, and lights on the
  pack make you visible from behind.
- Nights get cold — occasionally near freezing, and almost always chilly by 3am.
  Layer up BEFORE going out for the night and bring the warm coat you doubt you need.
- Be lit after dark, front and back — glow sticks or battery EL wire on your person.
  An unlit walker (a "darkwad") is the classic night hazard for bikes and art cars.
- Playa clothes never fully recover; assume whatever comes to the burn stays burner
  wardrobe. No need to overbuy: a basic base layer plus bold accessories reads as a
  full costume.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — Clothing & Costumes](https://www.burn.life/clothing--costumes.html) (Dr. Yes). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## Entry: the drive in [technique + tactics]
- Fuel discipline: top up in Gerlach (or Nixon on the way up) no matter what the
  gauge says. You want maximum range in the tank against a slow exodus at week's end.
- From the moment you leave I-80, drive exactly the limit — not one mph over. Local,
  county, and state patrols work that corridor hard, and a stop can become a search
  (K-9 units included). Do not pull onto soft shoulders; vehicles bog down instantly.
- Bike racks: if bikes hide the license plate, zip-tie the plate to the rearmost bike
  and light it after dark — an obscured plate is a classic pretext for a pull-over.
- Keep a full day of drinking water reachable in the cabin, even if the week's supply
  rides with someone else. Gate waits of 6+ hours happen at peak (roughly mid-day
  Sunday through Tuesday night), and weather closures have stretched waits far longer.
- No partying in the entry line — DUI law applies and is enforced there.
- Timing: arrive as the gates open, or from Wednesday on, for the shortest lines; and
  land with enough daylight left to build camp.
- Inside the city: 5 mph, watch for the unlit and the unsteady, park at camp, and the
  car stays parked until exodus.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — Getting to Burning Man (Entry)](https://www.burn.life/getting-to-burning-man-entry.html) (Dr. Yes). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## Exodus: leaving strategy [technique + tactics]
- The whole pain is one two-lane road. Departures from Sunday mid-morning through
  Monday risk the long queue — anywhere from 45 minutes to 8 hours, and unpredictable.
- The veteran windows: leave Saturday evening before the Man burns, or very early
  Sunday morning after it — both typically see minimal line.
- De-MOOP before you roll: sweep your footprint and take everything that is not playa
  dust. Garbage can be dropped in Gerlach for a few dollars a bag
  [era: 2014-2016 — verify price].
- Tune BMIR 94.5 FM for live wait estimates before committing to the line. If the
  estimate is ugly, an extra evening at camp with friends beats an evening in the
  queue.
- Pulsing: lanes stand fully stopped (engines off, stretch, meet the neighbors) for
  stretches, then release all at once — expect surges, not creep.
- Book the post-burn Reno hotel in advance; it is a holiday weekend and rooms sell
  out. The first shower and mediocre diner meal will feel like heaven.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — Leaving Burning Man (Exodus)](https://www.burn.life/leaving-burning-man-exodus.html) (Dr. Yes). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## RVs: power, capacity, and dust operations [technique]
- Generator sizing is about STARTING the air conditioner, not running it: start draw
  exceeds the advertised running draw, so you typically need at least 3,000 watts to
  kick an RV AC over. Choose an inverter generator — the quiet kind — over the loud
  contractor units rental companies push.
- "Sleeps 6" is a legal fiction of fold-out benches. Two people in a rental RV is
  comfortable; every body beyond that costs real livability and all privacy.
- Dust discipline: door closed always, shoes off at the step, clean up after storms
  before entering — and keep the ceiling vents SHUT unless you want a dune inside
  after the first blow.
- Black water is finite: many crews run a #1-only toilet rule to stretch it. Pump-out
  trucks do roam the city, but mid-week service is hit-or-miss — reserve with the
  service months ahead if the tank must last.
- Book early: California and Nevada rental fleets sell out around February. Delivered-
  to-playa RV packages start around $4,000 for the week [era: 2014-2016 — verify].
  Rent from a company that knows where the RV is going — the dust is unhideable.
- Budget packing-out time: an RV un-camps far slower than a tent.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — RVs](https://www.burn.life/rvs.html) and [Poopin' on the Playa](https://www.burn.life/poopin-on-the-playa.html) (Dr. Yes). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## Sanitation: beyond the porta-potty line [technique]
- The cold-3am answer is a dedicated pee jug in the tent: use it at night, pour it
  into a porta-potty later. Pour the CONTENTS only — never toss the jug itself in.
- Women: carry a pee funnel. Pee Funnel Camp gifts them free on playa, and camping
  stores sell reusable ones (She-Wee class). Veterans call this a week-changer.
- A real bucket toilet is legitimate: a sealable bucket with cat litter or dry soil
  absorbs and controls a #2. It leaves the playa WITH you for legal disposal at home —
  never buried, never in Gerlach bins, never in a regular dumpster.
- Camps can rent a private porta-potty from companies near Reno/Sparks
  [era: 2014-2016 — verify vendors], but only if the vendor can service it on playa;
  an unserviced private potty becomes an unusable biohazard by mid-week.
- Carry your own toilet paper and hand sanitizer — the public portas run out of both.
- Wipes and tampons never go down the hole: bag them (a clean-bag/dirty-bag pair
  inside one carrier bag works) and pack them out.
- Sit; do not hover. Close the lid. Everyone after you benefits.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — Poopin' on the Playa](https://www.burn.life/poopin-on-the-playa.html) (Dr. Yes). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## Cameras: dust discipline for photos [evergreen technique]
- Default state: camera sealed in a plastic bag, always, whenever it is not actively
  shooting. Never bring it out during a dust storm.
- Small sealed compact beats big glass on accessibility: a pocketable camera in a
  zip-bag in a hip pouch gets used constantly; a DSLR buried in a bagged backpack
  does not.
- Consider renting (with insurance) instead of risking an expensive unsealed body —
  post-burn cleanup of a rental is alcohol swabs and a return label.
- Telescoping zoom lenses pump dusty air into the body with every extend/retract
  cycle. Prefer internal-zoom or prime lenses, or baby the telescoper.
- Changing lenses: do it inside the tent or RV, inside a garbage bag nested in a
  second garbage bag, hands working within the bag. Dust on the sensor is forever
  (until a professional cleaning).
- Night shots need high-ISO performance, a fast lens, and usually a tripod; without
  those, shoot video instead or just put the camera down.
- People etiquette: ask before photographing anyone, and never publish shots of
  partially-dressed participants without explicit permission. Commercial or
  non-personal projects must follow the official Media Rights process.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — Cameras](https://www.burn.life/cameras.html) (Dr. Yes). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## Leave No Trace: a camp trash system that works [technique]
- Four containers, sorted at the moment of tossing: (1) burnables — paper, food
  scraps; (2) glass and plastic recyclables; (3) aluminum cans; (4) non-burnable
  trash. Color-code the bins and label them; collapsible laundry baskets pack flat.
- Unwrap everything at home before packing — packaging you never bring is MOOP you
  never manage.
- During the week: burnables go to burn barrels or the camp burn pit nightly;
  aluminum goes to Recycle Camp (the one recycling operation in the city); glass and
  plastic ride home — Reno redemption centers even pay for them.
- Done right, the drive home carries almost nothing but a light bag of true trash.
- Departure sweep: first each person combs their own site down to splinter and
  glitter scale, then the whole camp walks the footprint shoulder-to-shoulder in a
  line — twice. The cleanup volunteers who inspect afterward map every camp's MOOP
  (green/yellow/red), and the event's federal land permit literally depends on
  passing.
- Greywater — shower, dish, or wash water — never touches the playa.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — Leave No Trace](https://www.burn.life/leave-no-trace.html) (Dr. Yes, reprinting a system by burner ShiftyFox). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## Adventuring: the going-out kit [evergreen technique]
- The rule: go more than a street or two from camp and goggles, dust mask, and water
  come with you — no exceptions. Whiteouts do not schedule themselves.
- After dark add lighting visible from front AND back before leaving camp at all.
- Carry a reusable cup: camps and strangers offer drinks constantly, and nobody
  pours into cupped hands. Bars really do check ID — a photocopy taped to the cup
  means the real one stays safe at camp [note: some bars insist on the physical ID].
- Toilet paper and hand sanitizer live permanently in the day pack; the porta you
  need will be the one that ran out.
- Sun protection before leaving, every time. A playa burn is a week-ruiner.
- Navigate by landmarks that will not be burned down mid-week; the city is easy to
  read once you learn its clock-and-ring logic and very disorienting before that.
- In trouble? Find a Black Rock Ranger — the volunteers in khaki. They are not police
  and exist to help participants.
- Stopped art cars can be asked for a ride; that is what they are for.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — Adventuring on the Playa](https://www.burn.life/adventuring-on-the-playa.html) (Dr. Yes). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

## Budget: where the money actually goes [technique]
- Beyond ticket and transport, a modest-comfort tent week costs roughly $100-500 more
  depending on what can be borrowed [era: 2014-2016 — verify].
- The never-skip list, even at maximum cheapness: dust mask (a bandana counts),
  sealing goggles, night lights for your body, a way to carry water, and real warm
  clothing for the cold nights. These are safety, not comfort.
- Water is not a savings line: 1.5 gallons per person per day, extra if showering.
- A borrowed or secondhand tent is fine — spend the savings on anchoring (18"+
  stakes, rebar, or lag screws and rope). An Aluminet sheet is the budget shade that
  buys sleep past sunrise; camping under a friend's shade structure is even cheaper.
- The budget kitchen: small propane stove + one pot, boil-in-bag dinners cooked at
  home, instant oatmeal breakfasts, a week-long pasta salad for lunches.
- Free costumes exist on playa: outfitting camps (listed in the event guide) dress
  people for nothing, and thrift stores handle the rest — loud colors fit right in.
- Radical self-reliance is the budget's floor: arriving planning to live off other
  camps' food and water makes you a burden, not a burner. And never try to sneak in —
  vehicles are searched, the perimeter is watched at night, and a caught stowaway
  gets the entire vehicle's tickets voided.

*Credit: [Burn.Life — Burning on a Budget](https://www.burn.life/burning-on-a-budget.html) (Dr. Yes). Retrieved 2026-08-14.*

# The Man, the Temple, and how Burning Man started

## The Man [evergreen; 2026 burn night confirmed]
- The Man is the wooden effigy at the center of the clock face — the point every radial street aims at. The city is laid out around it.
- The Man burns Saturday night (September 5, 2026), after dark, with the Fire Conclave performing before the burn and a fire perimeter held until it drops. In recent years the burn has started around 9 pm; the exact 2026 time was not published on the pages checked. Big crowds, dust, and art cars — bring lights and agree on a meet-up spot with your camp beforehand.

## The Temple [2026-confirmed — Survival Guide "The Temple"]
- The Temple is a space for honoring, celebrating, grieving, and finding solace — memorials, quiet reflection, and sometimes weddings. It belongs to everyone; Temple Guardians keep it safe and welcoming from the moment it opens.
- Offerings: heartfelt tributes — photos, posters, messages, objects. Place them on any available surface inside, on the exterior walls, or on the surrounding fence, up to 10 feet high, without covering or climbing over another's tribute. Bring your own stapler or sturdy tape; the wind takes anything loose.
- Privacy and consent are the rule inside: photographing or recording other people or their offerings only with explicit prior consent, and that includes phones and smart glasses. Guardians remove threats, hate speech, desecration of others' offerings, weapons or intimidating objects, and safety hazards.
- The Temple burns Sunday night (September 6, 2026), after dark, in silence — no cheering, no fireworks; the whole city watches quietly. In recent years the Temple burn has started around 8 pm; exact 2026 time not published on the pages checked.
- The Temple sits on the open playa beyond the Man along the 12:00 axis. The first Temple was built in 2000 (David Best's Temple of the Mind); one has been built and burned every year since.

## History: how Burning Man started [evergreen — burningman.org Timeline + registry-verified]
- 1986: Larry Harvey and his friend Jerry James start Burning Man — they build an
  improvised wooden figure and burn it on Baker Beach in San Francisco on the
  Summer Solstice; a curious crowd gathers. That is the first Man. Burning Man
  started in 1986; it was founded by Larry Harvey and Jerry James; it started on
  Baker Beach, San Francisco, and moved to the desert in 1990. The founders of
  Burning Man are Larry Harvey and Jerry James. The year Burning Man started:
  1986. What year did it start? 1986, on Baker Beach.
- 1990: the last Baker Beach gathering — police stop the burn — and the event moves, with the Cacophony Society, to the Black Rock Desert in Nevada over Labor Day weekend. Black Rock City has risen on the Black Rock playa every year since, except 1997 (held nearby at Hualapai Playa / Fly Ranch) and 2020–2021 (cancelled for Covid-19). It returned in 2022.
- The 10 Principles were written by Larry Harvey in 2004 to describe the culture that had grown up (see the Ten Principles file). Today the city holds roughly 80,000 people at peak, and the two-lane highway in is the practical limit on its size.
- The event is put on by Burning Man Project, a nonprofit; the theme changes yearly (2026: "Axis Mundi").
